title: ITERTL An Iterative Framework for Fine-tuning LLMs for RTL Code Generation

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2, derivation preceding Equation 6 (knowledge-distillation reward analysis)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The derivation writes: 'min_π Σ_j -log P_π(a_j|s,a_{<j}) = min_π Σ_j log (P_teacher(a_j|s,a_{<j}) / log P_π(a_j|s,a_{<j}))'. The denominator inside the ratio incorrectly contains 'log P_π' instead of simply 'P_π'. The valid algebraic step (adding the π-independent constant log P_teacher to -log P_π) requires log(P_teacher/P_π), not log(P_teacher/log P_π); as written the expression is dimensionally and algebraically invalid, breaking the chain of equalities that leads to Equation 6.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2, line 2 of the derivation preceding Equation 6
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper equates 'Σ_j log(P_teacher(a_j|s,a_{<j})/P_π(a_j|s,a_{<j}))', a sum of log-ratios evaluated at the single realized token sequence a (sampled from π_teacher), directly to 'Σ_j KL(P_teacher,j || P_π,j)' using an exact '=' sign. True KL divergence is defined as an expectation over the full output distribution at each position, not the log-ratio evaluated at one sampled token. The paper itself notes that the subsequent step (turning this into an expectation over s and a) is only an approximation justified by the law of large numbers, which means the preceding line cannot simultaneously be an exact equality to the population-level KL divergence; the labeling of the sample-level quantity as 'KL' one line too early is a logical/notational error in the proof chain.

Section 2.1 states: 'VerilogEval[10] has released an open-source evaluation dataset, including 156 questions along with their corresponding golden solutions.' However, Section 4.1 describes VerilogEval as consisting of two separate sets: 'VerilogEval-machine, containing 143 samples' and 'VerilogEval-human, comprising 156 samples', i.e., 299 total questions. The earlier claim that the dataset includes '156 questions' materially understates and contradicts the later, more detailed description of the benchmark's actual size.

predicted_errors.error_location: Paper header/footer metadata (self-citation block and received/revised/accepted dates)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper's own citation reads 'Peiyang Wu ... 2018. ITERTL: An Iterative Framework for Fine-tuning LLMs for RTL Code Generation', and the footer states 'Received 20 February 2007; revised 12 March 2009; accepted 5 June 2009.' These dates (2007-2009, 2018) are temporally impossible given that the paper discusses DeepSeek-Coder-Instruct-6.7B, GPT-4, RTLCoder, and other 2023-2024 technologies, creating an internal inconsistency between the claimed publication timeline and the content described.

The paper states: 'the model is prompted to generate responses with temperature = {0 (greedy decoding), 0.2, 0.5, 0.8} and top_p = 0.95. For each test metric (pass@1, pass@5, and pass@10), the best result is chosen.' Selecting the maximum score across multiple decoding temperatures directly on the test benchmark (rather than fixing decoding hyperparameters a priori or tuning on a held-out validation set) constitutes test-set hyperparameter selection, which can inflate reported performance and is a methodologically questionable evaluation protocol.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 Training Details vs. Section 4.2 discussion of Figure 2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Training Details specify 'The total number of iterations is set to 7,' implying the final/reported model is the iteration-7 checkpoint. However, the Figure 2 discussion states that pass@1 peaks at iteration 5 and 'gradually decreases' from iteration 5 to 7, and separately claims 'with 5 iterations and only 10k reference data, our model beats the baseline model with 27k reference data.' This leaves it unclear whether the headline SOTA results in Table 1 (42.9%/62.2%) come from the degraded iteration-7 model (consistent with the stated 7-iteration training protocol) or the better-performing iteration-5 checkpoint, an internal inconsistency in which checkpoint underlies the reported results.
